name: Exogenous Work Assignment Institutional Treatment Qualification
text: Mellizo, Carpenter, and Matthews provide independent methodological evidence for Kaal's substrate-stage restriction. Their real-effort experiment randomly assigns manager and worker roles, keeps participants in a common production task, and makes participation in compensation governance exogenous to workers. The authors use this design to identify the causal effect of participatory authority and report output between seven and twelve percentage points higher in participatory firms. This supports the narrower proposition that exogenous work roles can hold the labor-allocation margin fixed while institutional authority varies. The comparison is limited. The source studies human workers in laboratory firms, varies compensation governance, and does not test agent labor markets, reputation, validation, staking, or the broader substrate. It therefore qualifies Kaal's identification strategy rather than validating the full architecture.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Participants are randomly assigned roles as managers or workers in firms that generate output via real effort. To identify the causal effect of participation on effort, workers are exogenously assigned to one of two treatments: one in which the manager implements a compensation scheme unilaterally or another in which the manager cedes control over compensation to the workers who vote to implement a scheme.

experiments allow one to implement exogenous, ceteris paribus changes. In our case, we compare groups of workers that were exogenously allowed (or not allowed) by a manager to participate in the running of the firm by having their vote determine the group’s compensation policy.
subjects were randomly assigned to one of the two roles by the computer program and informed of their job on their screen.
the only difference is that the vote counted in one treatment and it didn’t in the other
Given assignment to a participatory firm is exogenous, we can interpret the point estimate on the Participation treatment causally.
